segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: For all the frenzy on the screen, all the invitations to gawk, or be titillated, or outraged, or just shake your head in wonder, mostly it felt empty. It's tiring to watch, strangely tiring.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And it was awful. You know, it was just grim darkness. But then, somehow like the next day, Rosa was just pulling stuff out of the fridge to feed me with. And she pulls out the butter dish, you know? A glass butter dish. And it just shatters all over the floor.

segments.text: She drops it. And I just look at her, and I'm like, that was my dad's. (LAUGHING) It was just-- I was like, horrified! And my sister starts laughing, and I started laughing. Because it's not my dad's. It's just like a crappy butter dish from IKEA. And it was the first-- I think it was the first joke I remember. I remember it as the first joke of when my dad died.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's a study where scientists actually tried to quantify exactly how much time has to pass after tragedy before comedy kicks in. And although nothing is more tedious than people sitting around theorizing about what is funny, it's interesting to see somebody get super brass tacks about this and try to actually define this thing that our whole program is about today. These researchers had over 1,000 people rate how funny some joke tweets about Hurricane Sandy were at different points in time. And before the hurricane hit land, people thought the tweets were funny. And then, unsurprisingly, while the hurricane was destroying homes, and knocking out power, and killing people, and in the immediate aftermath of all that, the tweets did not seem funny and in fact seemed kind of offensive.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then, it took-- they have a number-- it took 15 days. 15 days after the hurricane struck, the tweets started to seem funny again. Because the researchers-- Peter McGraw, Lawrence Williams, and Caleb Warren-- theorize for something like this to be funny, it has to seem threatening, but not too threatening. Once it stops being threatening, it stops being funny. And in fact, there comes a point after the storm struck-- it is 36 days after the storm struck-- that people start finding the tweets less and less funny.

segments.text: And, to get back to Zoe, Zoe says, yeah, it was only a day after her dad's death that she joked about the butter dish. But the worst had already happened. The threat had past. segments.text: [CHUCKLES] Wow. This has gotten so real.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which brings us to this next story of a family, and something being too soon, and then knowing the right moment for the something to happen. We've arrived at Act 2 of our program. Act two, Pink Slip. When Amy Silverman was in her 20s, she had this friend who would go to LA sometimes and bring back these videos. And Amy and her friends would show the videos at parties. On VHS-- this is way back in the prehistoric days, before YouTube.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: This was the '90s. But in Phoenix. So it's probably like the '80s somewhere else.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And one of the films the guy would bring around to parties was called Pink Slip . Amy says she easily saw it a half dozen times, maybe it was more like a dozen. It always killed. Everybody liked it. It was an instructional video, and its lead character was this girl named Jill, who was just reaching puberty.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: I've never been able to figure out when exactly it was made. But probably like late '60s, early '70s. Kind of groovy living room, and they have very outdated hair. Very, very obviously staged. And that was what was so funny about it, really.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The film was about menstruation. And so if you're listening with a little kid right now, and you do not want to get into that subject with them right this second, take that into advisement. OK, here's a clip.

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: Susie, do you have periods?

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: Do I have periods? Jill, all women have periods about every four weeks for three or four days. When I'm on my period, blood from inside of my body comes outside from an opening between my legs.

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: Well, Susie, what about my teacher? Does Miss Jones have periods?

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: Yes, Jill. Your teacher, Mrs. Jones, does have periods. All women have periods about every four weeks for three or four days.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Hi, girls.

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: Hi, Dad.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: What have you girls been talking about?

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: About periods, Daddy! Dad, does Aunt Carol have periods?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yes, Jill. All women have periods about every four weeks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So it's very repetitive.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: And we would watch it and shriek with laughter. Not proud of it, but that is what happened. A lot.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Blood from inside a woman's body comes outside, from an opening between her legs, about every four weeks.

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: But the blood? Won't it get on my clothes?

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: No, it won't. Because you use a sanitary pad.

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: A sanitary pad.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Amy says it did register with her that there was something up with that girl, Jill. Something different. But she never really gave it much thought. And she and her friends would drink, and they'd watch this kitschy old film. And years later, when Amy was 37, she had her second child-- a daughter, Sophie. And Sophie had Down Syndrome.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: So when Sophie was like two weeks old, all of a sudden I was driving down the street one day, and I went, oh my god, Pink Slip ! And suddenly, it all came together for me, and I realized that that video had been about a girl with Down Syndrome. And now I had a baby with Down Syndrome. And some day, I was going to have to figure out how to teach her about puberty. And then, as quickly as that thought came into my head, I shoved it out and replaced it with, I don't know, a need for diapers or something.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Years pass, and by the time Sophie was 10, she had seen her older sister become an adolescent, and Sophie was obsessed.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: She had a bra collection. She had a deodorant collection.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Not that she needed a bra or deodorant just yet, Amy says. There was one false alarm, where it seemed like she was growing hair in new places.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: And she started jumping up and down. She ran down the hallway naked into her sister's room to show her. She grabbed my cell phone and called one of my friends, and she raced around the kitchen table as fast as she could, again and again, you know, just talking about her hair with my mom, with my friend, with my husband.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, she really wants to hit puberty.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: She really wants to hit puberty.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Amy and her husband decided to enroll Sophie in a class about puberty, a one-time seminar for kids with Down Syndrome, to answer their questions and teach them what they needed to know about what was going to happen to them, taught by this woman who is an expert on all that. And it was OK. It was fine. Though it didn't do the job for Sophie.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Sophie was-- you know, she was about to turn 12, and she was still asking questions.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What were the questions she was asking?

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: She wanted to know the basics about her period. About where the blood would come out, what she would use. Just basics. And I thought, you know what? Maybe I should show her Pink Slip.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This was honestly something she had never considered before. She'd never taken that video seriously.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: No. No! We made fun of it. So I got the video up for her, for her to see.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, I know you recorded a conversation with her before you showed her the video. Let me just play that piece of tape. Here we go.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Do you remember what we're talking about today?

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: Periods.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Yep. And now, do you feel like you already know everything about them?

segments.speaker: Sophie
segments.text: Yup. Because last year, I had a puberty lesson. And they sang a song-- "Just Around the Corner."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She's saying last year they did a puberty lesson, and they sang a song-- "Just Around the Corner." That's how she knows everything. Amy pulled up Pink Slip on her phone because, of course, it's on YouTube.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: And, unlike me, Sophie loves to watch videos on YouTube. So she grabbed it and watched it.

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: And so let's watch the video.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: So let's watch the video?

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: Yes, what about periods?

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: Do you have periods?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the recording that Amy made of Sophie watching Pink Slip, there is a moment where they both laugh. It's the most shocking moment in the film, and it really is kind of shocking. Again, if you are listening right now with a small child, know that I am about to say something very frank about menstruation. And just decide if you want to keep listening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The moment that Amy and Sophie laugh at in the video is one that Amy remembers very well from back when she used to watch the video with her friends at parties. It's kind of the big moment in the film.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Well, this was like the grabber at the parties. Where Jill would say to Susie, you know, I don't understand or something. And Susie would say, well, come into the bathroom with me, Jill. I have my period right now. And then sit down, and pull down her pants, and show her bloody pad.

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: This is a used sanitary pad.

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: Look, there's blood on it.

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: See?

segments.speaker: Jill
segments.text: You mean the blood's coming from inside your body now?

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: That's right.

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: [SNICKERS]

segments.speaker: Susie
segments.text: Blood is coming from inside my body through an opening between my legs.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: For the record, I laughed first.

segments.speaker: Sophie
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Just a minute later, after the sister shows the girl in the film how to throw away a used pad and start using a new pad, Sophie watches intently and quietly says--

segments.speaker: Sophie
segments.text: I get it now.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Back at the parties that Amy used to go to, when the scene drew the biggest laughs and the most comments, it was just too soon for Amy to get what the video would be good for-- for a girl like Sophie.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What was it like watching her watch this video that you knew so well?

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Completely surreal. Completely surreal. I mean, embarrassing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Why was it embarrassing?

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Oh, I was embarrassed because I used to make fun of it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But Sophie didn't know that.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: No, but I don't feel like that really honored her. You know? My prior behavior.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, I see what you're saying. Here you are. You've got this little girl who you love. And now, with her present, you're returning to the scene of the crime.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Yeah. I felt more ashamed than embarrassed. But I had to stop and think, huh, maybe the person who made that video really knew what they were doing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. That's the thing I was wondering, is did it give you a respect for the video?

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: It did. It was really weird.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so all the corny repetition in the whole thing, that's totally right for her.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: That's what she needs. It just has to be slowed down. The learning has to be slowed down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you feel like a certain amount of being a parent is realizing what an ass you were before you were a parent?

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Yes. Absolutely. I mean, I was the one who-- I always tell people this. I was the one who would switch lines at Safeway if there was a person with a developmental disability bagging groceries. Because I just didn't want to deal. It would've taken, what? 15 seconds to nod and smile? And be a human being about it? Not me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Amy's thought about showing Pink Slip to Sophie again. It's been a few months, and Sophie still has not gotten her period. Though Amy's not sure what Sophie would think of the video today. Because Sophie's able to tell that the girl in the video has Down Syndrome. And Sophie is going through a thing right now where she does not like to identify herself that way.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Not to get all serious on you, but Sophie is starting to realize that she's-- she's not going to ever have some of the things that her sister has. So recently, she asked me, am I going to have Down Syndrome when I grow up? And I said, you are. And she said, I don't want to. I don't want to have it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what does her sister get that she doesn't get, that she sees right now?

segments.speaker: Amy Silverman
segments.text: She gets to go to a fancy art school that won't take Sophie. She gets to dance on point in ballet, which Sophie doesn't get to do because her feet aren't strong enough. She gets sleepover invitations Sophie doesn't get. And she gets that life in front of her. You know, she-- Sophie told me the other day that she doesn't want to have an aid at school anymore, because she wants to practice walking to class by herself for college.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What Sophie will get that her sister got, and she'll probably get it pretty soon, is her period. And Amy might show her Pink Slip again. Amy tried once to show the video to Sophie's older sister. And the older sister got to the part with the bloody pad and then tossed the phone back to Amy. But Sophie's different, and she liked the video. Pink Slip was what she needed.
